The inverse ZZ-polynomial of a matroid

Alice L.L. Gao1, Xuan Ruan2 and Matthew H.Y. Xie3

1,2Shenzhen Research Institute of Northwestern Polytechnical University,

Sanhang Science &\& Technology Building, No. 45th, Gaoxin South 9th Road, Nanshan District, Shenzhen City, 518057, P.R. China

1,2School of Mathematics and Statistics,

Northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi’an, Shaanxi 710072, P.R. China

3College of Science,

Tianjin University of Technology, Tianjin 300384, P. R. China

Email: 1llgao@nwpu.edu.cn, 2ruanxuan1211@163.com, 3xie@email.tjut.edu.cn

Abstract. Motivated by the ZZ-polynomials of matroids, Ferroni, Matherne, Stevens, and Vecchi introduced the inverse ZZ-polynomial of a matroid. In this paper, we prove several fundamental properties of the inverse ZZ-polynomial, including non-negativity and multiplicativity, and show that it is a valuative invariant. We also provide explicit formulas for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of uniform matroids and a broader class of matroids, namely sparse paving matroids, which include uniform matroids as a special case. Furthermore, we establish the unimodality and log-concavity of these polynomials in the case of sparse paving matroids. Based on the properties of the ZZ-polynomial, we conjecture that the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial are unimodal and log-concave.

AMS Classification 2020: 05B35, 52B40, 05A20

Keywords: inverse ZZ-polynomial, valuative invariant, uniform matroid, sparse paving matroid, log-concavity.

Corresponding Author: Matthew H.Y. Xie, xie@email.tjut.edu.cn

1 Introduction

Since the introduction of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials of matroids by Elias, Proudfoot, and Wakefield [5], these polynomials have attracted much attention. For instance, see [4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 19] and references therein. In [20], Proudfoot, Xu, and Young introduced the ZZ-polynomial Z𝖬​(t)Z_{\mathsf{M}}(t) of a matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, which is defined as the weighted sum of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials for all possible contractions of 𝖬\mathsf{M}. They also demonstrated that, for realizable matroids, the coefficients of Z𝖬​(t)Z_{\mathsf{M}}(t) can be interpreted as the intersection cohomology Betti numbers of a projective variety. A precise description of this intersection cohomology for any matroid was later provided by Braden, Huh, Matherne, Proudfoot, and Wang [3]. Within the framework of Kazhdan-Lusztig-Stanley theory, Ferroni, Matherne, Stevens, and Vecchi [7] introduced the inverse ZZ-polynomial of a matroid. Their work in [7] primarily focuses on the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the Chow rings and augmented Chow rings of matroids and does not pay much attention to the inverse ZZ-polynomials, despite their many interesting properties that are worth further exploration. The main objective of this paper is to compute the inverse ZZ-polynomials of uniform matroids and sparse paving matroids. In addition, we study the unimodality and log-concavity of the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids.

Let us first recall some basic definitions related to the inverse ZZ-polynomials of matroids. For readers unfamiliar with matroids, we recommend Oxley’s book [18] on matroid theory for background. Throughout this paper, we adopt the notions and notation used in Ferroni, Matherne, Stevens, and Vecchi [7]. Let 𝖬=(E,B)\mathsf{M}=(E,{B}) denote a matroid, where EE is the ground set and B{B} is the set of all bases of 𝖬\mathsf{M}. The rank of a subset A⊆EA\subseteq E is defined by rk⁡(A):=maxB∈B⁡|A∩B|\rk(A):=\max_{B\in{B}}|A\cap B|, and the rank of 𝖬\mathsf{M} is given by rk⁡(𝖬):=rk⁡(E).\rk(\mathsf{M}):=\rk(E). A flat of 𝖬\mathsf{M} is a subset F⊆EF\subseteq E such that either F=EF=E or the rank of FF strictly increases upon adding new elements. The set of all flats of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, ordered by inclusion, forms a lattice, denoted by ℒ⁡(𝖬)\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}). For any subset A⊆EA\subseteq E, the restriction of 𝖬\mathsf{M} to AA is denoted 𝖬|A\mathsf{M}|_{A}, and the contraction of 𝖬\mathsf{M} by AA is denoted 𝖬/A\mathsf{M}/A. Let P𝖬​(t)P_{\mathsf{M}}(t) and Q𝖬​(t)Q_{\mathsf{M}}(t) denote the Kazhdan-Lusztig and inverse Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, respectively. Given a loopless matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the ZZ-polynomial of 𝖬\mathsf{M} is defined as

Z𝖬​(t):=∑F∈ℒ⁡(𝖬)trk⁡(𝖬|F)​P𝖬/F​(t)\displaystyle Z_{\mathsf{M}}(t):\,=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M})}t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}|_{F})}P_{\mathsf{M}/F}(t) (1)

by Proudfoot, Xu, and Young [20]. Working in the incidence algebra framework, Ferroni, Matherne, Stevens, and Vecchi [7, p.25] introduced a related polynomial Y^𝖬​(t)\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}}(t), defined by

Y^𝖬​(t):=∑F∈ℒ⁡(𝖬)(−1)rk⁡(𝖬|F)​Q𝖬|F​(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬/F)​μ𝖬/F,\displaystyle\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}}(t):\,=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M})}(-1)^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}|_{F})}Q_{\mathsf{M}|_{F}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}/F)}\mu_{\mathsf{M}/F}, (2)

where μ𝖬=μ⁡[∅,E]\mu_{\mathsf{M}}=\mu[\emptyset,E] is the Möbius invariant of 𝖬\mathsf{M}. We define the inverse ZZ-polynomial of 𝖬\mathsf{M} by

Y𝖬​(t):=(−1)rk⁡(𝖬)​Y^𝖬​(t).\displaystyle Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t):=(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M})}\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}}(t). (3)

This modification ensures that Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) has non-negative coefficients, as shown in Proposition 2.1, rather than Y^𝖬​(t)\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}}(t). For matroids with loops, we define Y𝖬​(t):=Y𝖬∖{loops}​(t).Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t):=Y_{\mathsf{M}\setminus\text{\lx@text@lbrace loops\lx@text@rbrace}}(t). Since ZZ-polynomials and inverse ZZ-polynomials of matroids are defined in a similar manner, it is natural to ask whether they share common properties. In addition to the non-negativity of the coefficients, we also establish that the inverse ZZ-polynomials of matroids are palindromic, as shown in Lemma 2.2, and multiplicative under direct sums, as shown in Proposition 2.3, which mirror the well-known properties of the ZZ-polynomials of matroids.

In this paper, we first focus on computing explicit expressions for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of uniform matroids and sparse paving matroids. Let 𝖴k,n\mathsf{U}_{k,n} denote the uniform matroid of rank kk on nn elements, where the ground set is E=[n]E=[n] and the set of bases is B=([n]k){B}=\binom{[n]}{k}. The first main result is the following theorem.

Theorem 1.1

For any uniform matroid 𝖴k,n\mathsf{U}_{k,n} with n≥k≥1n\geq k\geq 1, we have

Y𝖴k,n​(t)=∑i=0⌊k/2⌋(ni)​(n−i−1n−k)​ti+∑i=0⌊(k−1)/2⌋(ni)​(n−i−1n−k)​tk−i.Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{i}\binom{n-i-1}{n-k}t^{i}+\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{i}\binom{n-i-1}{n-k}t^{k-i}.

To compute the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids, we first prove that the inverse ZZ-polynomial is a valuative invariant.

Theorem 1.2

The assignment 𝖬→Y𝖬​(t)\mathsf{M}\rightarrow Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) is a valuative invariant.

The explicit formula for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids is given by the following expression.

Theorem 1.3

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be a sparse paving matroid of rank kk and cardinality nn. Suppose 𝖬\mathsf{M} has λ\lambda circuit-hyperplanes. Then

Y𝖬​(t)=Y𝖴k,n​(t)−λ⁡((1+t)k−12​((−1)k+1)​Ck2​tk2),Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t)-\lambda\left((1+t)^{k}-\frac{1}{2}\left((-1)^{k}+1\right)C_{\frac{k}{2}}t^{\frac{k}{2}}\right),

where Cn=1n+1​(2​nn)C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n} is the nn-th Catalan number.

The second part of this paper explores the unimodality and log-concavity of inverse ZZ-polynomials. Recall that a polynomial f⁡(t)=a0+a1​t+⋯+an​tn∈ℝ⁡[t]f(t)=a_{0}+a_{1}t+\cdots+a_{n}t^{n}\in\mathbb{R}[t] is unimodal if there exists an index 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n such that

a0≤a1≤⋯≤ai≥ai+1≥⋯≥an.a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{i}\geq a_{i+1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{n}.

A polynomial is log-concave if

ai2≥ai−1​ai+1a_{i}^{2}\geq a_{i-1}a_{i+1}

for all 0<i<n,0<i<n, and it has no internal zeros if there do not exist indices 0≤i<j<k≤n0\leq i<j<k\leq n such that ai,ak≠0a_{i},a_{k}\neq 0 and aj=0a_{j}=0. Additionally, a polynomial is said to be real-rooted if all of its roots are real, or if f⁡(t)=0f(t)=0. For a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients, if it has only real roots, then its coefficients are log-concave and have no internal zeros; in particular, they form a unimodal sequence. Proudfoot, Xu, and Young [20] conjectured that for any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the roots of its ZZ-polynomial Z𝖬​(t)Z_{\mathsf{M}}(t) lie exclusively on the negative real axis. However, computational experiments show that the inverse ZZ-polynomials may not always have real roots. We make the following conjectures for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of matroids.

Conjecture 1.4

For any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) are unimodal.

Conjecture 1.5

For any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) form a log-concave sequence with no internal zeros.

Based on Theorem 1.3, we prove that Conjecture 1.4 and 1.5 hold for sparse paving matroids, as stated in the following theorem.

Theorem 1.6

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be a sparse paving matroid of rank kk and cardinality nn. Then

  • (1)(1)

    the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) are unimodal;

  • (2)(2)

    the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) form a log-concave sequence with no internal zeros.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we establish several properties of the inverse ZZ-polynomials of matroids, including their non-negativity and multiplicativity. In Section 3, we first review the basic definitions of matroid polytopes, subdivisions, and valuations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the inverse ZZ-polynomial of a matroid is a valuative invariant. In Section 4, we provide an explicit expression for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of uniform matroids. In Section 5, we derive a general formula for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids. In Section 6, we prove the unimodality and log-concavity of the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids.

2 Inverse ZZ-polynomials of matroids

In this section, we study several key properties of the inverse ZZ-polynomials of matroids, analogous to those of matroid ZZ-polynomials.

We first establish the non-negativity of the coefficients of ZZ-polynomials. Braden, Huh, Matherne, Proudfoot, and Wang [3] showed that the coefficients of matroid ZZ-polynomials are non-negative. A similar result holds for inverse ZZ-polynomials:

Proposition 2.1

For any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) are non-negative.

Proof.

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be a loopless matroid. Recall from Proudfoot [19] that its characteristic polynomial is defined as

χ𝖬​(t)=∑F∈ℒ⁡(𝖬)μ𝖬|F​trk⁡(𝖬/F).\displaystyle\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M})}\mu_{\mathsf{M}|_{F}}t^{\rk(\mathsf{M}/F)}. (4)

The polynomial χ𝖬​(t)\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(t) is monic of degree rk⁡(𝖬)\rk(\mathsf{M}), and its constant term is the Möbius invariant μ𝖬\mu_{\mathsf{M}}. Considering the alternating signs in χ𝖬​(t)\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(t) (see [21, Theorem 4]), we deduce that μ𝖬\mu_{\mathsf{M}} is (−1)rk⁡(𝖬)(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M})} multiplied by a positive integer.

Since the inverse Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial Q𝖬​(t)Q_{\mathsf{M}}(t) has non-negative coefficients, it follows directly from (2) that each summation term

(−1)rk⁡(𝖬|F)​Q𝖬|F​(t)​trk⁡(𝖬/F)​μ𝖬/F(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M}|_{F})}Q_{\mathsf{M}|_{F}}(t)\,t^{\rk(\mathsf{M}/F)}\mu_{\mathsf{M}/F}

in the definition of Y^𝖬​(t)\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}}(t) is (−1)rk⁡(𝖬)(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M})} times a polynomial with non-negative coefficients. Thus, the polynomial Y𝖬​(t)=(−1)rk⁡(𝖬)​Y^𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M})}\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}}(t) has non-negative coefficients. ∎

With non-negativity established, we turn to palindromicity. It is known that matroid ZZ-polynomials are palindromic [20]. Braden, Huh, Matherne, Proudfoot, and Wang [3, p.5] observed that inverse ZZ-polynomials also share this property; thus, we state the result without proof.

Lemma 2.2

For any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) is palindromic of degree rk⁡(𝖬)\rk(\mathsf{M}), i.e.,

trk⁡(𝖬)​Y𝖬​(t−1)=Y𝖬​(t).t^{\rk(\mathsf{M})}Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t^{-1})=Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t).

We now demonstrate that the inverse ZZ-polynomial of a matroid is multiplicative with respect to direct sums. The direct sum of two matroids 𝖬1=(E1,B1)\mathsf{M}_{1}=(E_{1},{B}_{1}) and 𝖬2=(E2,B2)\mathsf{M}_{2}=(E_{2},{B}_{2}), where E1∩E2=∅E_{1}\cap E_{2}=\emptyset, is defined on the ground set E1∪E2E_{1}\cup E_{2} with the set of bases

B1∪B2={B1∪B2:B1∈B1,B2∈B2}.{B}_{1}\cup{B}_{2}=\{B_{1}\cup B_{2}:B_{1}\in{B}_{1},B_{2}\in{B}_{2}\}.

It is a well-known fact that the (inverse) Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials and the ZZ-polynomials of matroids are all multiplicative under direct sums; see [5], [13], and [20], respectively. The corresponding result for inverse ZZ-polynomials is as follows.

Proposition 2.3

For any matroids 𝖬1\mathsf{M}_{1} and 𝖬2\mathsf{M}_{2} with respective ground sets E1E_{1} and E2E_{2}, we have

Y𝖬1⊕𝖬2​(t)=Y𝖬1​(t)⋅Y𝖬2​(t).Y_{\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t)=Y_{\mathsf{M}_{1}}(t)\cdot Y_{\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t).
Proof.

The statement can be proven in the same manner as Elias, Proudfoot and Wakefield did for the matroid Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials. From (3), it suffices to show that

Y^𝖬1⊕𝖬2​(t)=Y^𝖬1​(t)​Y^𝖬2​(t).\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t)=\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}}(t)\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t).

We proceed by induction on the sum rk⁡(𝖬1)+rk⁡(𝖬2)\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{1})+\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{2}). The statement is clear when rk⁡(𝖬1)=0\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{1})=0 or rk⁡(𝖬2)=0\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{2})=0. Now, assume that the statement holds for 𝖬1′\mathsf{M}_{1}^{\prime} and 𝖬2′\mathsf{M}_{2}^{\prime} whenever one of rk⁡(𝖬1′)≤rk⁡(𝖬1)\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{1}^{\prime})\leq\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{1}) and rk⁡(𝖬2′)≤rk⁡(𝖬2)\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{2}^{\prime})\leq\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{2}), with strict inequalities in at least one of the ranks.

By the properties of flats, we have

ℒ⁡(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)=ℒ⁡(𝖬1)×ℒ⁡(𝖬2)andrk⁡(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)=rk⁡(𝖬1)+rk⁡(𝖬2).\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})=\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{1})\times\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{2})~~~~~~\text{and}~~~~~~\mathrm{rk}\,(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})=\mathrm{rk}\,(\mathsf{M}_{1})+\mathrm{rk}\,(\mathsf{M}_{2}).

Moreover, for any (F1,F2)∈ℒ⁡(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)(F_{1},F_{2})\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2}),

(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)|(F1,F2)\displaystyle(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})|_{(F_{1},F_{2})} =(M1|F1)⊕(𝖬2|F2),\displaystyle=(M_{1}|_{F_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}|_{F_{2}}),
(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)/(F1,F2)\displaystyle(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})/{(F_{1},F_{2})} =(𝖬1/F1)⊕(𝖬2/F2).\displaystyle=(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}}).

Hence, using (2), we obtain

Y^𝖬1⊕𝖬2​(t)\displaystyle\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t) =∑(F1,F2)∈ℒ⁡(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)Q^(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)|(F1,F2)​(t)⋅trk⁡((𝖬1⊕𝖬2)/(F1,F2))​μ(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)/(F1,F2)\displaystyle=\sum_{(F_{1},F_{2})\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})}\hat{Q}_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})|_{(F_{1},F_{2})}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}\left((\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})/{(F_{1},F_{2})}\right)}\mu_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})/{(F_{1},F_{2})}}
=∑(F1,F2)∈ℒ⁡(𝖬1⊕𝖬2)Q^(𝖬1|F1)⊕(𝖬2|F2)​(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬1/F1)+rk⁡(𝖬2/F2)​μ(𝖬1/F1)⊕(𝖬2/F2).\displaystyle=\sum_{(F_{1},F_{2})\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2})}\hat{Q}_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}|_{F_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}|_{F_{2}})}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}}\right)+\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}}\right)}\mu_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}})}.

By the inductive hypothesis, we get

Y^𝖬1⊕𝖬2​(t)\displaystyle\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t) =Q^(𝖬1|E1)⊕(𝖬2|E2)​(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬1/E1)+rk⁡(𝖬2/E2)​μ(𝖬1/E1)⊕(𝖬2/E2)\displaystyle=\hat{Q}_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}|_{E_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}|_{E_{2}})}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{E_{1}}\right)+\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{E_{2}}\right)}\mu_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{E_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{E_{2}})}
+∑(F1,F2)≠(E1,E2)Q^(𝖬1|F1)⊕(𝖬2|F2)(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬1/F1)+rk⁡(𝖬2/F2)μ(𝖬1/F1)⊕(𝖬2/F2)\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{(F_{1},F_{2})\neq(E_{1},E_{2})}\hat{Q}_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}|_{F_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}|_{F_{2}})}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}}\right)+\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}}\right)}\mu_{(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}})\oplus(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}})}
=Q^𝖬1⊕𝖬2​(t)\displaystyle=\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t)
+∑(F1,F2)≠(E1,E2)(Q^𝖬1|F1(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬1/F1)μ𝖬1/F1)⋅(Q^𝖬2|F2(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬2/F2)μ𝖬2/F2),\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{(F_{1},F_{2})\neq(E_{1},E_{2})}\left(\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}|_{F_{1}}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}}\right)}\mu_{\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}}}\right)\cdot\left(\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}|_{F_{2}}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}\left(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}}\right)}\mu_{\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}}}\right), (5)

where the last identity follows from the fact that the Möbius invariants of matroids are multiplicative under direct sums, as shown in [22, Theorem 7.1.7.]. On the other hand, by (2), we have

Y^𝖬1​(t)\displaystyle\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}}(t) =∑F1∈ℒ⁡(𝖬1)Q^𝖬1|F1​(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬1/F1)​μ𝖬1/F1,\displaystyle=\sum_{F_{1}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{1})}\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}|_{F_{1}}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}})}\mu_{\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}}},
Y^𝖬2​(t)\displaystyle\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t) =∑F2∈ℒ⁡(𝖬2)Q^𝖬2|F2​(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬2/F2)​μ𝖬2/F2,\displaystyle=\sum_{F_{2}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M}_{2})}\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}|_{F_{2}}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}})}\mu_{\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}}},

which leads to

Y^𝖬1​(t)⋅Y^𝖬2​(t)=Q^𝖬1​(t)⋅Q^𝖬2​(t)\displaystyle\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}}(t)\cdot\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t)=\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}}(t)\cdot\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t)
+∑(F1,F2)≠(E1,E2)(Q^𝖬1|F1(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬1/F1)μ𝖬1/F1)⋅(Q^𝖬2|F2(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬2/F2)μ𝖬2/F2).\displaystyle\quad+\sum_{(F_{1},F_{2})\neq(E_{1},E_{2})}\left(\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}|_{F_{1}}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}})}\mu_{\mathsf{M}_{1}/{F_{1}}}\right)\cdot\left(\hat{Q}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}|_{F_{2}}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}})}\mu_{\mathsf{M}_{2}/{F_{2}}}\right). (6)

Subtracting (6) from (5) yields

Y^𝖬1⊕𝖬2​(t)−Y^𝖬1​(t)​Y^𝖬2​(t)=0.\displaystyle\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}\oplus\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t)-\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{1}}(t)\hat{Y}_{\mathsf{M}_{2}}(t)=0.

This completes the proof. ∎

3 Matroid polytopes, subdivisions, and valuations

The aim of this section is to prove Theorem 1.2. To this end, we first review the basic definitions of matroid polytopes, subdivisions, and valuations, primarily following the notions and notation summarized by Ferroni and Schröter [9].

Let 𝖬=(E,B)\mathsf{M}=(E,{B}) be a matroid. For each i∈Ei\in E, let eie_{i} denote the ii-th canonical vector in ℝE\mathbb{R}^{E}. The base polytope of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, denoted by P⁡(𝖬){P}(\mathsf{M}), is defined as the convex hull of the set of vectors eBe_{B}, where each B∈BB\in{B} is a base of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, and eB=∑i∈Beie_{B}=\sum_{i\in B}e_{i}. That is,

P⁡(𝖬):=conv​{eB:B∈B}⊆ℝE.{P}(\mathsf{M}):=\text{conv}\{e_{B}:B\in{B}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{E}.

A subdivision of P=P⁡(𝖬)⊆ℝE{P}={P}(\mathsf{M})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{E} is a finite collection 𝒮={P1,P2,…,Ps}\mathcal{S}=\{{P}_{1},{P}_{2},\ldots,{P}_{s}\} of matroid polytopes Pi=P⁡(𝖬i)⊆ℝE{P}_{i}={P}(\mathsf{M}_{i})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{E}, such that the following conditions hold:

  • •

    P=⋃i=1sPi{P}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{s}{P}_{i}.

  • •

    Any face of a polytope Pi∈𝒮{P}_{i}\in\mathcal{S} is contained in some polytope in 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

  • •

    For each pair of distinct indices i≠ji\neq j, the intersection Pi∩Pj{P}_{i}\cap{P}_{j} is a common (possibly empty) face of both Pi{P}_{i} and Pj{P}_{j}.

Sometimes, when dealing with a subdivision 𝒮\mathcal{S} of a matroid polytope P{P}, it is convenient to focus only on the interior faces of the subdivision. More precisely, if we denote the boundary of P{P} by ∂P\partial{P}, we define

𝒮int:={Pi∈𝒮:Pi⊈∂P}.\mathcal{S}^{\operatorname{int}}:=\{{P}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}:{P}_{i}\not\subseteq\partial{P}\}.

Throughout this paper, we consider matroids with ground sets of the form E⊆ℤ≥1E\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}, where |E|<∞|E|<\infty. For any such EE, let ℳE\mathcal{M}_{E} denote the set of all base polytopes of matroids on EE, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be the union of all the ℳE\mathcal{M}_{E}’s. Let AA be an abelian group (typically a ring). Consider a map f:ℳ→Af:\mathcal{M}\to A. If f⁡(P⁡(𝖬))=f⁡(P⁡(N))f\left({P}(\mathsf{M})\right)=f\left({P}(\mathrm{N})\right) whenever 𝖬≅N\mathsf{M}\cong\mathrm{N}, we say that ff is an invariant. If ff satisfies the following property for every matroid polytope P{P} and every subdivision 𝒮={P1,P2,…,Ps}\mathcal{S}=\{{P}_{1},{P}_{2},\ldots,{P}_{s}\} of P{P}, i.e.,

f⁡(P)=∑Pi∈𝒮int(−1)dim⁡P−dim⁡Pi​f​(Pi),f({P})=\sum_{{P}_{i}\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{int}}}(-1)^{\operatorname{dim}{P}-\operatorname{dim}{P}_{i}}f({P}_{i}),

we say that ff is a valuation. To simplify our notation, we will use f⁡(𝖬)f(\mathsf{M}) to denote the map f:ℳ→Af:\mathcal{M}\to A instead of writing f⁡(P⁡(𝖬))f({P}(\mathsf{M})).

In order to prove Theorem 1.2, we first need to establish the following basic lemma on matroid valuative invariants, which has appeared in several previous works. For the sake of completeness, we provide a self-contained proof.

Lemma 3.1

If f:ℳ→ℝ⁡[t]f:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[t] is a valuative invariant, then the maps g1,g2:ℳ→ℝ⁡[t]g_{1},g_{2}:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[t] defined by

g1​(𝖬)=trk⁡(𝖬)​f​(𝖬)andg2​(𝖬)=(−1)rk⁡(𝖬)​f​(𝖬),\displaystyle g_{1}(\mathsf{M})=t^{\rk(\mathsf{M})}f(\mathsf{M})~~~~~~~~~~\text{and}~~~~~~~~~~g_{2}(\mathsf{M})=(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M})}f(\mathsf{M}),

are both valuative invariants

Proof.

Since f:ℳ→ℝ⁡[t]f:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[t] is a valuative invariant, we have

f⁡(𝖬)=∑P⁡(𝖬i)∈𝒮int(−1)dim⁡P⁡(𝖬)−dim⁡P⁡(𝖬i)​f​(𝖬i)f\left(\mathsf{M}\right)=\sum_{{P}(\mathsf{M}_{i})\in\mathcal{S}^{\mathrm{int}}}(-1)^{\operatorname{dim}{P}(\mathsf{M})-\operatorname{dim}{P}(\mathsf{M}_{i})}f(\mathsf{M}_{i})

for any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M} and any subdivision 𝒮={P⁡(𝖬1),P⁡(𝖬2),…,P⁡(𝖬s)}\mathcal{S}=\{{P}(\mathsf{M}_{1}),{P}(\mathsf{M}_{2}),\ldots,{P}(\mathsf{M}_{s})\} of P=P⁡(𝖬){P}={P}(\mathsf{M}) in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Note that all matroids corresponding to the polytopes in 𝒮\mathcal{S} share the same ground set and rank. Therefore, we have

trk⁡(𝖬)=trk⁡(𝖬i)and(−1)rk⁡(𝖬)=(−1)rk⁡(𝖬i)t^{\rk(\mathsf{M})}=t^{\rk(\mathsf{M}_{i})}\quad\text{and}\quad(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M})}=(-1)^{\rk(\mathsf{M}_{i})}

for each 𝖬i\mathsf{M}_{i}. The desired result then follows, which completes the proof. ∎

Let RR be a ring and let f,g:ℳ→Rf,g:\mathcal{M}\to R be two maps. The convolution of ff and gg, denoted by f⋆g:ℳ→Rf\star g:\mathcal{M}\to R, is defined as

(f⋆g)​(𝖬):=∑S⊆Ef⁡(𝖬|S)​g​(𝖬/S),(f\star g)(\mathsf{M}):=\sum_{S\subseteq E}f(\mathsf{M}|_{S})g(\mathsf{M}/S),

where 𝖬\mathsf{M} is a matroid with ground set EE. It is worth noting that if g:ℳ→Rg:\mathcal{M}\to R satisfies g⁡(𝖬)=0g(\mathsf{M})=0 whenever 𝖬\mathsf{M} contains loops, the convolution of any other invariant ff with gg depends only on the flats of 𝖬\mathsf{M}. Specifically, we have

(f⋆g)​(𝖬)=∑F∈ℒ⁡(𝖬)f⁡(𝖬|F)​g​(𝖬/F),(f\star g)(\mathsf{M})=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M})}f(\mathsf{M}|_{F})g(\mathsf{M}/F),

since the contraction 𝖬/S\mathsf{M}/S is loopless if and only if SS is a flat. One of the main results of Ardila and Sanchez [1] establishes that the convolution of two valuations is itself a valuation, as stated in the following theorem.

Theorem 3.2 ([1], Theorem C)

Let RR be a ring. If f,g:ℳ→Af,g:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow A are valuations, then the convolution f⋆gf\star g is also a valuation.

We are now ready to prove that the inverse ZZ-polynomial is a valuative invariant.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let f,g:ℳ→ℝ⁡[t]f,g:\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}[t] be defined by

f⁡(𝖬)=(−1)rk⁡(𝖬)​Q𝖬​(t)andg⁡(𝖬)=trk⁡(𝖬)​μ𝖬.f(\mathsf{M})=(-1)^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M})}Q_{\mathsf{M}}(t)\quad\text{and}\quad g(\mathsf{M})=t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M})}\mu_{\mathsf{M}}.

It is known from Ardila and Sanchez [1, Theorem 8.8] that the map 𝖬→Q𝖬​(t)\mathsf{M}\rightarrow Q_{\mathsf{M}}(t) is a valuative invariant. By applying Lemma 3.1, it follows that ff is also a valuative invariant. Furthermore, recall that the Tutte polynomial T𝖬​(x,y)T_{\mathsf{M}}(x,y) of a matroid 𝖬=(E,B)\mathsf{M}=(E,{B}) is defined as

T𝖬​(x,y):=∑A⊆E(x−1)rk⁡(E)−rk⁡(A)​(y−1)|A|−rk⁡(A)∈ℤ⁡[x,y].T_{\mathsf{M}}(x,y):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}(x-1)^{\mathrm{rk}(E)-\mathrm{rk}(A)}(y-1)^{|A|-\mathrm{rk}(A)}\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y].

There are several established proofs showing that the map ℳ→ℤ⁡[x,y]\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}[x,y] defined by f:𝖬→T𝖬​(x,y)f:\mathsf{M}\rightarrow T_{\mathsf{M}}(x,y) is a valuative invariant; see [9, Theorem 7.17]. From the identity

χ𝖬​(t)=(−1)rk⁡(𝖬)​T𝖬​(1−t,0),\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=(-1)^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M})}T_{\mathsf{M}}(1-t,0),

we deduce that both the characteristic polynomial χ𝖬​(t)\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(t) and the Möbius invariant μ𝖬=χ𝖬​(0)\mu_{\mathsf{M}}=\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(0) are valuative invariants. Again, by Lemma 3.1, we conclude that gg is a valuative invariant as well. It is worth noting that g=trk⁡(𝖬)​μ𝖬=0g=t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M})}\mu_{\mathsf{M}}=0 whenever 𝖬\mathsf{M} has loops. Combining this with Theorem 3.2, we obtain the following expression for the convolution

(f⋆g)​(𝖬)\displaystyle(f\star g)(\mathsf{M}) =∑F∈ℒ⁡(𝖬)f⁡(𝖬|F)​g​(𝖬/F)\displaystyle=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M})}f(\mathsf{M}|_{F})g(\mathsf{M}/F)
=∑F∈ℒ⁡(𝖬)(−1)rk⁡(F)​Q𝖬|F​(t)⋅trk⁡(𝖬/F)​μ𝖬/F\displaystyle=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{L}(\mathsf{M})}(-1)^{\mathrm{rk}(F)}Q_{\mathsf{M}|_{F}}(t)\cdot t^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M}/F)}\mu_{\mathsf{M}/F}
=(−1)rk⁡(𝖬)​Y𝖬​(t),\displaystyle=(-1)^{\mathrm{rk}(\mathsf{M})}Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t),

which is a valuative invariant. This completes the proof. ∎

4 Uniform matroids

The aim of this section is to compute the inverse ZZ-polynomials of uniform matroids. To this end, we first provide the expression for μ𝖬\mu_{\mathsf{M}} in the case of uniform matroids.

Lemma 4.1 ([22, p.121])

For any uniform matroid 𝖴k,n\mathsf{U}_{k,n} with n≥k≥1n\geq k\geq 1, its Möbius invariant satisfies

μ𝖴k,n=(−1)k​(n−1k−1).\displaystyle\mu_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}=(-1)^{k}\binom{n-1}{k-1}. (7)

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.1, which presents an explicit formula for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of uniform matroids.

From Lemma 2.2, we know that for any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}, the polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) is palindromic of degree rk⁡(𝖬)\rk(\mathsf{M}). Here, BnB_{n} denotes the Boolean matroid, a special uniform matroid of rank nn and cardinality nn for n≥1n\geq 1, and B0B_{0} denotes the unique matroid of rank 0. Moreover, there exist (ni)\binom{n}{i} such flats. For i=ki=k, there exists only one flat of rank kk, which is the ground set EE. Hence, we have

for n>k≥1n>k\geq 1; see [13, Theorem 3.3]. Substituting equations (7), (9), and (10) into (8), we obtain

⌊k/2⌋<k−⌊(k−1)/2⌋.\lfloor k/2\rfloor<k-\lfloor(k-1)/2\rfloor.

Therefore, for any 0≤i≤⌊k/2⌋0\leq i\leq\lfloor k/2\rfloor, the coefficient of tit^{i} in Y𝖴k,n​(t)Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t) is (ni)​(n−i−1n−k).\binom{n}{i}\binom{n-i-1}{n-k}. Thus, we complete the proof. ∎

5 Sparse paving matroids

This section is dedicated to proving Theorem 1.3. In fact, based on Theorem 1.2, we derive a general formula for the inverse ZZ-polynomials of large classes of matroids, including elementary split matroids and (sparse) paving matroids.

Let us first review the definitions of elementary split matroids and (sparse) paving matroids. Let 𝖬=(E,B)\mathsf{M}=(E,{B}) be a matroid. An independent set of 𝖬\mathsf{M} is a set I⊆EI\subseteq E contained in some B⊆BB\subseteq{B}. If a set is not independent, we will say that it is dependent. A circuit of 𝖬\mathsf{M} is a minimal dependent set. A matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M} is called paving if all its circuits have size at least rk⁡(𝖬)\rk(\mathsf{M}). If both 𝖬\mathsf{M} and its dual 𝖬∗\mathsf{M}^{*} are paving, then 𝖬\mathsf{M} is referred to as a sparse paving matroid. A well-known conjecture by Mayhew, Newman, Welsh, and Whittle [17] affirms that asymptotically, almost all matroids are sparse paving. The class of elementary split matroids is somewhat more complicated to define. First introduced in [2], they form a subclass of the split matroids introduced by Joswig and Schröter in [16]. Ferroni and Schröter [9] conjectured that the class of elementary split matroids is strictly larger than the class of sparse paving matroids. It is expected that elementary split matroids will dominate even when considering only non sparse paving matroids.

The aforementioned classes of matroids can be equivalently defined through the relaxation of stressed subsets. Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be a matroid on the ground set EE with rank kk. A subset A⊆EA\subseteq E is called stressed if both the restriction 𝖬|A\mathsf{M}|_{A} and the contraction 𝖬/A\mathsf{M}/A are isomorphic to uniform matroids. Ferroni and Schröter [9, Section 3] describe how to construct a new matroid on EE by relaxing a stressed subset AA, which generalizes the well-known circuit-hyperplane relaxation (A flat of rank rk⁡(𝖬)−1\rk(\mathsf{M})-1 is said to be a hyperplane). Precisely, the cusp of AA is defined as the collection of kk-sets

cusp𝖬⁡(A):={S∈(Ek):|S∩A|≥rk⁡(A)+1},\cusp_{\mathsf{M}}(A):=\left\{S\in\binom{E}{k}:|S\cap A|\geq\rk(A)+1\right\},

and a new matroid is constructed on the ground set EE whose family of bases is given by B∪cusp𝖬⁡(A){B}\cup\cusp_{\mathsf{M}}(A). This matroid is referred to as the relaxation of 𝖬\mathsf{M} by AA and is denoted by Rel⁡(𝖬,A)\Rel(\mathsf{M},A). If AA and A′A^{\prime} are two distinct stressed subsets of 𝖬\mathsf{M}, then A′A^{\prime} remains stressed in Rel⁡(𝖬,A)\Rel(\mathsf{M},A), and the cusp of A′A^{\prime} in Rel⁡(𝖬,A)\Rel(\mathsf{M},A) is given by cusp𝖬⁡(A′)\cusp_{\mathsf{M}}(A^{\prime}). In particular, for each matroid, one may associate a canonical relaxed matroid, obtained by relaxing (in any order) all stressed subsets with non-empty cusp. The following proposition provides equivalent definitions of the previously discussed classes of matroids in terms of the relaxation of stressed subsets. For further details, we refer to [8, Corollary 3.17], [9, Theorem 4.8], and [10, Lemma 5.1].

Proposition 5.1

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be a matroid of rank kk on the ground set E=[n]E=[n].

  • (1)(1)

    𝖬\mathsf{M} is sparse paving if and only if the relaxation of all of its circuit-hyperplanes yields the matroid 𝖴k,n\mathsf{U}_{k,n}.

  • (2)(2)

    𝖬\mathsf{M} is paving if and only if the relaxation of all of its stressed hyperplanes of size at least kk yields the matroid 𝖴k,n\mathsf{U}_{k,n}.

  • (3)(3)

    𝖬\mathsf{M} is elementary split if and only if the relaxation of all of its stressed subsets with non-empty cusp yields the matroid 𝖴k,n\mathsf{U}_{k,n}.

In a direct sum of two uniform matroids, the ground sets of each of the summands are stressed and therefore can be relaxed. For 0≤r≤h0\leq r\leq h and 0≤k−r≤n−h0\leq k-r\leq n-h, Ferroni and Schröter [9] defined the cuspidal matroid Λr,k,h,n:=Rel⁡(𝖴k−r,n−h⊕𝖴r,h,𝖴r,h),\mathsf{\Lambda}_{r,k,h,n}:=\Rel(\mathsf{U}_{k-r,n-h}\oplus\mathsf{U}_{r,h},\mathsf{U}_{r,h}), i.e., they relaxed the subset corresponding to the ground set of the direct summand 𝖴r,h\mathsf{U}_{r,h}. We have the following general expression for Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) when 𝖬\mathsf{M} is an elementary split matroid.

Proposition 5.2

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be an elementary split matroid of rank kk and cardinality nn. Then

Y𝖬​(t)=Y𝖴k,n​(t)−∑r,hλr,h​(YΛr,k,h,n​(t)−Y𝖴k−r,n−h​(t)⋅Y𝖴r,h​(t))Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t)-\sum_{r,h}\lambda_{r,h}\left(Y_{\Lambda_{r,k,h,n}}(t)-Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k-r,n-h}}(t)\cdot Y_{\mathsf{U}_{r,h}}(t)\right)

where λr,h\lambda_{r,h} denotes the number of stressed subsets with non-empty cusp of size hh and rank rr in 𝖬\mathsf{M}.

Proof.

For any valuative invariant ff and elementary split matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M} of rank kk and cardinality nn, it is known from Ferroni and Schröter [9, Theorem 5.3] that

f⁡(𝖬)=f⁡(𝖴k,n)−∑r,hλr,h​(f⁡(Λr,k,h,n)−f⁡(𝖴k−r,n−h⊕𝖴r,h)).f(\mathsf{M})=f(\mathsf{U}_{k,n})-\sum_{r,h}\lambda_{r,h}\left(f(\mathsf{\Lambda}_{r,k,h,n})-f(\mathsf{U}_{k-r,n-h}\oplus\mathsf{U}_{r,h})\right).

Since the inverse ZZ-polynomial is a valuative invariant by Theorem 1.2 and is multiplicative under direct sums of matroids by Lemma 2.3, applying these properties to the above identity yields the desired result. ∎

When 𝖬\mathsf{M} is a paving matroid, the expression for Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) in Proposition 5.2 simplifies as follows.

Proposition 5.3

Let 𝖬\mathsf{M} be an paving matroid of rank kk and cardinality nn. Then

Y𝖬​(t)=Y𝖴k,n​(t)−∑h≥kλh​(Y𝖴k,h+1​(t)−(1+t)⋅Y𝖴k−1,h​(t)),Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t)-\sum_{h\geq k}\lambda_{h}\left(Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,h+1}}(t)-(1+t)\cdot Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k-1,h}}(t)\right),

where λh\lambda_{h} denotes the number of stressed hyperplanes of size hh in 𝖬\mathsf{M}.

Proof.

In a paving matroid of rank kk, the only stressed subsets with non-empty cusp are the stressed hyperplanes of size at least kk. Since the rank of any hyperplane is k−1k-1, we have the following expression for the inverse ZZ-polynomial of 𝖬\mathsf{M},

Y𝖬​(t)=Y𝖴k,n​(t)−∑h≥kλh​(YΛk−1,k,h,n​(t)−Y𝖴1,n−h​(t)⋅Y𝖴k−1,h​(t)).Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t)-\sum_{h\geq k}\lambda_{h}\left(Y_{\Lambda_{k-1,k,h,n}}(t)-Y_{\mathsf{U}_{1,n-h}}(t)\cdot Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k-1,h}}(t)\right).

From Ferroni, Nasr, and Vecchi [8, Proposition 3.11], we know that the simplification of the cuspidal matroid Λk−1,k,h,n\Lambda_{k-1,k,h,n} is isomorphic to the uniform matroid 𝖴k,h+1\mathsf{U}_{k,h+1}. Since the inverse ZZ-polynomials remain invariant under taking simplifications of loopless matroids, it follows that

YΛk−1,k,h,n​(t)=Y𝖴k,h+1​(t).Y_{\Lambda_{k-1,k,h,n}}(t)=Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,h+1}}(t).

Moreover, by Theorem 1.1, we have Y𝖴1,n−h​(t)=1+t.Y_{\mathsf{U}_{1,n-h}}(t)=1+t. Combining these results, we obtain the desired expression for Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t), completing the proof. ∎

We now proceed to give a proof of Theorem 1.3.

Y𝖬​(t)=Y𝖴k,n​(t)−λ⁡(Y𝖴k,k+1​(t)−(1+t)⋅Y𝖴k−1,k​(t)).\displaystyle Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t)=Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t)-\lambda\left(Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,k+1}}(t)-(1+t)\cdot Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k-1,k}}(t)\right).

6 Unimodality and Log-Concavity

This section is dedicated to proving Theorem 1.6, which demonstrates that the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids are both unimodal and log-concave.

We have already established in Proposition 2.1 that the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) for any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M} are non-negative. Based on this result, we now present a new proof of the non-negativity of the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids, derived through direct calculation.

Second proof of Proposition 2.1 in the case of sparse paving matroids.

From Corollary 5.4 and Remark 5.5, it suffices to show that

(nk)​(ki)​(k−in−i−λ∗)≥0\binom{n}{k}\binom{k}{i}\left(\frac{k-i}{n-i}-\lambda^{*}\right)\geq 0

for 0≤i≤k2.0\leq i\leq\frac{k}{2}. Note that for any two positive integers 2≤a≤b2\leq a\leq b, we have ab≥a−1b−1.\frac{a}{b}\geq\frac{a-1}{b-1}. Thus, it follows that

k−in−i≥k−i−1n−i−1≥⋯≥1n−k+1.\displaystyle\frac{k-i}{n-i}\geq\frac{k-i-1}{n-i-1}\geq\cdots\geq\frac{1}{n-k+1}. (17)

On the other hand, from [9, Corollary 4.13], we have λ≤(nk)​min⁡{1k+1,1n−k+1},\lambda\leq\binom{n}{k}\min\left\{\frac{1}{k+1},\frac{1}{n-k+1}\right\}, which implies

λ∗=λ(nk)≤min⁡{1k+1,1n−k+1}≤1n−k+1.\displaystyle\lambda^{*}=\frac{\lambda}{\binom{n}{k}}\leq\min\left\{\frac{1}{k+1},\frac{1}{n-k+1}\right\}\leq\frac{1}{n-k+1}. (18)

Combining (17) and (18), we obtain

k−in−i−λ∗≥0\displaystyle\frac{k-i}{n-i}-\lambda^{*}\geq 0 (19)

for each 0≤i≤k20\leq i\leq\frac{k}{2}. Hence, the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomials of sparse paving matroids are non-negative. ∎

Proudfoot, Xu, and Young [20] proved that the coefficients of the ZZ-polynomial of a realizable matroid can be interpreted as the intersection cohomology Betti numbers of a projective variety. Later, in the work of Braden, Huh, Matherne, Proudfoot, and Wang [3], a more precise description of the intersection cohomology was obtained for any matroid 𝖬\mathsf{M}. This naturally leads to the following question.

Problem 1. Do the coefficients of the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) have a geometric interpretation?

Now, we proceed to prove Theorem 1.6, which demonstrates that Conjecture 1.4 and 1.5 hold for sparse paving matroids.

A property known as γ\gamma-positivity, which implies symmetry and unimodality, has recently attracted attention in topological, algebraic, and enumerative combinatorics. We recall that a polynomial f⁡(t)=∑iai​ti∈ℝ⁡[t]f(t)=\sum_{i}a_{i}t^{i}\in\mathbb{R}[t] is said to be γ\gamma-positive if it can be expressed as

f⁡(t)=∑i=0⌊n2⌋γi​ti​(1+t)n−2​i,f(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor}\gamma_{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i},

where n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and γ0,γ1,…,γ⌊n2⌋\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor} are non-negative real numbers. Ferroni and Schröter [9] proved that the ZZ-polynomials of matroids are γ\gamma-positive. Since Y𝖬​(t)Y_{\mathsf{M}}(t) is a palindromic polynomial, it is natural to investigate its γ\gamma-positive property. However, we argue that the inverse ZZ-polynomial Y𝖴k,n​(t)Y_{\mathsf{U}_{k,n}}(t) of a matroid is not necessarily γ\gamma-positive. As an example, consider the uniform matroid 𝖴4,5\mathsf{U}_{4,5}. According to Theorem 1.1, the inverse ZZ-polynomial of 𝖴4,5\mathsf{U}_{4,5} is given by Y𝖴4,5​(t)=4​t4+15​t3+20​t2+15​t+4.Y_{\mathsf{U}_{4,5}}(t)=4t^{4}+15t^{3}+20t^{2}+15t+4. Upon calculation, we find that the associated γ\gamma-polynomial is γ⁡(Y𝖴4,5​(t),t)=−2​t2−t+4.\gamma(Y_{\mathsf{U}_{4,5}}(t),t)=-2t^{2}-t+4. Since the coefficients of this γ\gamma-polynomial are not all non-negative, it follows that Y𝖴4,5​(t)Y_{\mathsf{U}_{4,5}}(t) is not γ\gamma-positive.
